column1: What is a Wireshark "capture"?
column2: A recording of every packet your network interface saw, saved so you can inspect them one by one

column1: What file format does Wireshark save captures in?
column2: .pcapng — the standard capture format you can reopen and share

column1: What does promiscuous mode do?
column2: Makes your network card copy ALL traffic passing by, not just packets addressed to you

column1: Keyboard shortcut to start/stop a capture?
column2: Ctrl+E (Cmd+E on Mac)

column1: How do you spot the right interface to capture on the Wireshark start screen?
column2: The one with an activity graph (a moving waveform) next to it — that's your active connection

column1: What is Npcap (the Windows installer option)?
column2: The driver that lets Wireshark listen to your network card on Windows

column1: On a typical home Wi-Fi, whose traffic does your Wireshark capture see?
column2: Mostly your own device's traffic — other devices' packets generally don't pass by your radio

column1: What is a "packet"?
column2: A small chunk of data sent over the network — one row in Wireshark's packet list

column1: Name the three panes of the Wireshark window
column2: Packet List (top), Packet Details (middle), Packet Bytes (bottom)

column1: True or false: the three panes always describe the same packet
column2: True — selecting a row updates all three panes

column1: What's the difference between a "frame" and a "packet" in Wireshark?
column2: For beginners: same row, synonyms. Precisely: "frame" is the whole unit as it went on the wire; "packet" is loose everyday speech

column1: List the nested layers of a web packet, outside-in
column2: Frame → Ethernet → IP → TCP → HTTP

column1: What does the Ethernet layer of a packet tell you?
column2: Hardware (MAC) addressing between devices on your local network

column1: What happens in the Packet Bytes pane when you highlight a layer in Packet Details?
column2: The corresponding bytes light up in the hex view

column1: What does a black packet with red text in the packet list mean?
column2: Wireshark detected a problem (e.g., a checksum error) — take it seriously

column1: What is a TCP "pure ACK" packet (and its default color)?
column2: A tiny acknowledgment packet ("yep, got it") — purple

column1: What do the Time column's display modes change?
column2: What the numbers mean: seconds since capture start, time of day, or seconds since the previous packet

column1: What does a display filter do?
column2: Hides packets you don't want to see — nothing is deleted and it's fully reversible

column1: What do green and red mean in the display filter bar?
column2: Green = valid syntax applied; red = malformed filter, did nothing

column1: Display filter: show only DNS packets
column2: dns

column1: Display filter: traffic to OR from 192.168.1.10
Display filter: only the opening SYN of a new connection
column2: tcp.flags.syn == 1 && tcp.flags.ack == 0

column1: Filter operators for and / or / not?
column2: && / || / ! (plus parentheses for grouping)

column1: What does "Apply as Filter" (right-click a field) do?
column2: Builds a display filter from the exact field you clicked — no typing needed

column1: Capture-filter (BPF) equivalents of: ip.addr == 1.2.3.4 and tcp.port == 443
column2: host 1.2.3.4 and tcp port 443

column1: Key difference between display filters and capture filters?
column2: Display filters what you SEE (reversible). A capture filter drops packets BEFORE they're recorded — gone forever

column1: Rule of thumb for using filters?
column2: Capture everything, narrow with display filters — use capture filters only when recording everything is impractical

column1: Display filter: only failed web requests
column2: http.response.code >= 400

column1: How do you save a filter for one-click reuse?
column2: Right-click the filter bar → Manage Filter Favorites → add it (becomes a button)

column1: What does DNS do?
column2: Translates names like example.com into IP addresses like 93.184.216.34 — the internet's phone book

column1: Which transport and port does DNS normally use?
column2: UDP port 53

column1: What pairs a DNS query with its response?
column2: The Transaction ID — matches like a ticket number

column1: What is an A record?
column2: The DNS answer mapping a name to an IPv4 address

column1: What is a CNAME record?
column2: An alias pointing one name to another name — answers can chain through aliases before reaching an address

column1: What is TTL in a DNS answer?
column2: Time to live — how many seconds the answer may be cached

column1: Display filter: DNS lookups slower than 100 ms
column2: dns.time > 0.1

column1: Symptom: DNS queries with no responses — what does the user experience?
column2: The site won't load — a DNS failure, even though the network is fine

column1: Why might revisiting a website show NO DNS traffic in your capture?
column2: The answer is still cached — your computer remembers it until the TTL expires

column1: The TCP three-way handshake, in order?
column2: SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK

column1: What does a SYN packet mean?
column2: Let's start a connection — my starting sequence number is X

column1: Why do both sides of a TCP connection send sequence numbers?
column2: Each side keeps its own byte-counter, so lost or out-of-order data can be detected and re-sent in order

column1: How do port numbers identify programs?
column2: The server listens on a well-known port (80 = HTTP); your side uses a random high port — together with IPs they identify the conversation

column1: What does right-click → Follow → TCP Stream do?
column2: Reassembles both directions of a conversation into one readable transcript, with each side in its own color

column1: What does a polite TCP connection close look like?
column2: FIN, ACK packets — a mutual, four-packet hang-up

column1: What does a TCP RST flag mean?
column2: Abort — hang up NOW, something is wrong

column1: When does the actual HTTP request happen relative to the handshake?
column2: Only AFTER all three handshake packets — data rides packets flagged PSH, ACK

column1: What does an HTTP GET request mean?
column2: Please send me this resource — method + path + version, e.g., GET / HTTP/1.1

column1: What is the HTTP POST method used for?
column2: Sending data TO the server (forms, logins, uploads)

column1: What does the Host header specify?
column2: Which website on that server you want — one server can host many sites

column1: The four HTTP status-code families?
column2: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client's fault, 5xx server's fault

column1: What does HTTP 404 mean?
column2: Resource not found (4xx = your side's fault)

column1: What does the Content-Type header tell you?
column2: What kind of data follows (text/html, image/png, application/json...)

column1: Display filter: all HTTP requests (not responses)
column2: http.request

column1: Why doesn't https://example.com traffic show under the "http" filter?
column2: It's TLS-encrypted — Wireshark can't parse it as HTTP, so it shows as TLS instead

column1: Why can't you read the contents of HTTPS in Wireshark?
column2: TLS encrypts everything before it hits the network — the recorded bytes are scrambled

column1: Which part of an HTTPS connection is still readable in a capture?
column2: The TLS handshake: Client Hello, Server Hello, Certificate — all in cleartext

column1: What is SNI?
column2: Server Name Indication — the target site's name sent in plaintext in the Client Hello; it leaks which sites you visit

column1: What's in the server's TLS certificate?
column2: The server's name, the signing authority, and the expiry — your browser validates it automatically

column1: What can a network observer STILL see with HTTPS?
column2: Destination IP, site name (via SNI), the DNS lookup, and timing/size patterns

column1: What can an observer NOT see with HTTPS?
column2: URLs, page contents, passwords, cookies, form data

column1: What does "Application Data" in the Info column mean?
column2: Encrypted payload — opaque binary, nothing readable

column1: How can Wireshark decrypt your own TLS traffic (advanced technique)?
column2: Point it at your browser's session-key log via the SSLKEYLOGFILE environment variable — only works for traffic where you control an endpoint

column1: Is analyzing other people's network traffic without permission legal?
column2: No — wiretapping laws apply even if the traffic is unencrypted

column1: What does Statistics → Protocol Hierarchy show?
column2: What fraction of packets and bytes each protocol makes up — the fastest fingerprint of a capture

column1: What is a "conversation" in Statistics → Conversations?
column2: One pair of addresses talking; sort by Bytes to find the big players of the capture

column1: Conversations vs. Endpoints — what's the difference?
column2: Conversations group traffic by PAIR of addresses; Endpoints group by a single address

column1: What does the IO Graph plot?
column2: Packets or bytes per second across the capture's timeline — the traffic's heartbeat

column1: Three "shapes of trouble" visible in an IO Graph?
column2: Dead silence (disconnection), sawtooth bursts-and-stalls (retransmissions), one channel saturating (bandwidth hog)

column1: What lives in Statistics → Capture File Properties?
column2: Duration, packet/byte totals, and the capture comments field — always annotate saved captures

column1: What can you do by right-clicking something in a statistics screen?
column2: Apply as Filter — pivot straight from the statistic to the actual packets

column1: The three usual suspects when "the network feels slow"?
column2: Slow DNS, packet loss (retransmissions), refused/reset connections

column1: Display filter: find slow DNS lookups
column2: dns.time > 0.1 — anything over 100 ms is a smoking gun

column1: What causes TCP retransmissions?
column2: Packet loss on the path — the receiver's duplicate ACKs tell the sender to re-send the missing data

column1: Display filter: find retransmissions
column2: tcp.analysis.retransmission

column1: What are duplicate ACKs?
column2: The receiver re-acknowledging data it already has — the "still missing that piece" signal that precedes a retransmission

column1: What does an RST in reply to your SYN mean?
column2: Connection refused — nothing is listening on that port, or a firewall rejected you

column1: Display filter: find connection resets
column2: tcp.flags.reset == 1

column1: Where should Wireshark troubleshooting START?
column2: View → Expert Information — Wireshark's own warning list, linking straight to the offending packets

column1: The three-step diagnostic workflow?
column2: Orient with statistics → suspect with filters → prove with specific packets

column1: What does "passing" a capstone diagnosis require?
column2: Naming the right suspect AND citing your evidence — the filter you used and the packet numbers

column1: What is the actual professional skill the capstone drilled?
column2: Turning "a capture happened" into "here are the three things this capture is about," backed by evidence
